--- title: "Thanksgiving Dinner, Measured in Hours of Work" subtitle: "The Farm Bureau's basic $55 dinner isn't what most families spend. But because it's the same menu every year, it shows something real: it takes less work than ever." author: "SixtyEight95" date: "2026-11-18" categories: [groceries, holidays, cost of living, wages] image: infographic.png --- ::: {.cell} ::: Every November, the American Farm Bureau Federation shops for the same classic Thanksgiving dinner for 10: a 16-pound turkey, stuffing, sweet potatoes, rolls, peas, cranberries, a veggie tray, pumpkin pie with whipped cream, and milk and coffee. They've done it every year since 1986. The dollar price has roughly doubled since then. But that's only half the story. So, as usual, we asked: **how long does the average worker have to work to buy it?** ## The short answer ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} In 2025, the Farm Bureau's **basic** dinner for 10 cost **$55.18** on average nationally (about **$83–85** in the Northeast and West). That's a bare-bones menu, not a typical family's grocery bill: no ham, no mashed potatoes, no drinks. But because it's the **same menu every year**, it's a fair way to track the trend. At the average worker's pay, it took **1.7 hours of work** in 2025, the least in the survey's 40-year history. In 1986, it took 3.2 hours. ::: ## Wait, $55 for 10 people? That was our reaction too. Here's exactly what the Farm Bureau's shopping list includes, and what it leaves out: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Included in the $55 |Not included | |:---------------------------------------------|:-----------------------| |16-lb turkey |ham | |14-oz box of stuffing |mashed potatoes | |3 lbs sweet potatoes |mac and cheese | |12 rolls |green bean casserole | |1 lb frozen peas |gravy beyond the basics | |12 oz cranberries |appetizers | |small veggie tray |drinks and alcohol | |2 pumpkin pies (canned filling, store crusts) |extra desserts | |whipped cream |leftovers | |1 gallon of milk | | |coffee and baking basics | | ::: ::: A few more reasons the number looks low: - **It's a national average.** The same dinner cost about **$83** in the Northeast and **$85** in the West. Prices in the South and Midwest pull the average down. - **Turkey is often a loss leader.** Stores frequently discount turkeys before Thanksgiving to get shoppers in the door, and the survey catches some of those deals. - **Portions are modest.** One box of stuffing and a pound of peas for 10 people is not most families' idea of a feast. So think of the $55 as a **price index**, not a budget. Your real dinner probably costs more, maybe much more. What the survey is good for is comparing **the same basket** across years. ## 40 years of Thanksgiving dinner ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Hover to see the price each year. The dollar cost peaked at **$64.05** in 2022, when inflation and bird flu sent turkey prices soaring. That year dinner took 2.3 hours of work, a visible bump. Since then, the price has fallen three years in a row while pay kept rising, so dinner got easier to afford on both counts. ## Dollars vs. work ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Year | Dinner for 10| Average hourly pay| Hours of work| Minutes per guest| |:----|-------------:|------------------:|-------------:|-----------------:| |1986 | $28.74| $9.01| 3.2| 19| |1995 | $29.64| $11.78| 2.5| 15| |2005 | $36.78| $16.30| 2.3| 14| |2015 | $50.11| $21.21| 2.4| 14| |2019 | $48.91| $23.83| 2.1| 12| |2022 | $64.05| $28.11| 2.3| 14| |2025 | $55.18| $31.79| 1.7| 10| ::: ::: In dollars, Thanksgiving is about twice as expensive as in 1986. In work time, it's about half the work. ## What about this year? The Farm Bureau releases its 2026 survey the week before Thanksgiving. We'll update this post when it comes out. With food prices rising again this fall, we'll be watching to see whether the streak of cheaper dinners holds. ## The fine print - **One menu, national average.** The survey prices the same classic menu every year; your actual dinner, store, and region will differ. Regional prices in the Northeast and West run well above the national average. - **A few early years are estimates.** The year-by-year series we used fills a few early gaps using inflation data; the Farm Bureau's own figures anchor the start and recent years. - **Pay is the average worker's hourly earnings in November**, before taxes, for the roughly 80% of private-sector workers who aren't managers. ## The bottom line The Farm Bureau's $55 dinner is a bare-bones basket, and your real Thanksgiving almost certainly costs more. But tracking that same basket for 40 years shows something real: measured in the time it takes to earn it, the basic Thanksgiving dinner was more affordable last year than at any point since the survey began, about **10 minutes of work per guest.** --- **How we did this.** Dinner costs are the American Farm Bureau Federation's annual Thanksgiving Dinner Cost Survey (classic menu for 10). Years 1987–2022 come from a compilation by 24/7 Wall St.; 1986 and 2023–2025 are from AFBF. Pay is average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees for November of each year, via [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/AHETPI). [AFBF survey](https://www.fb.org/market-intel/thanksgiving-dinner-cost-analysis-moderate-decline)
